 Inside Revolut's product marketing engine Subscribe Sign in Inside Revolut's product marketing engine An in-depth conversation with Revolut’s Head of Product Marketing, Sophie Storey Rory Woodbridge Jul 23, 2026 25 6 Share Revolut is one of the most remarkable companies Europe has ever produced. Very few businesses can boast the kind of scale, shipping velocity, or revenue growth enjoyed by the London-founded fintech. It’s a company I’ve long admired, and from a product marketing perspective, one does have to wonder: how do you run a PMM function at that pace, across that many products and countries, without the quality of the work dropping? So I sat down with Sophie Storey, Head of Product Marketing at Revolut. Sophie joined as the third PMM a few years ago. Today she leads 27 product marketers from Brazil to Spain to the UK. A few things stood out from the chat. The team has landed on a success metric for product marketing that has actually stuck, including a novel “GTM Excellence” score. Sophie has systematised how a large, global team uses AI, and she’s clear-eyed about where it helps and where it doesn’t. She also reflected on what’s changed as the team has scaled - a reminder that the shape and remit of a PMM team is always evolving. Check out the full interview below. Let’s start with the stats. How big is the product marketing team at Revolut? And how is it structured? We’re currently at 27 product marketers, and I’ve got 15 new roles open on my screen as we speak. That sounds like a lot, but for the number of products and the revenue overall, it’s still pretty lean. The model is one, maybe two PMMs per product department, plus a core PMM team that sits with me. When I joined I was the third PMM. Since then we’ve moved from GTM-over-everything to owning the full arc, we look at product adoption and driving ongoing usage, not just the launch. Most PMMs sit directly in their product departments. Everyone at Revolut has a line manager and a functional manager. Your line manager is usually the head of product, setting priorities and guiding the roadmap. The functional manager is me or someone on my team, looking after the quality of the work and whether you’re growing as a PMM. That split lets PMMs be embedded as strategic partners, while we keep the bar on the craft. Where does PMM actually sit? Is brand under you, or separate? The core PMM team sits in a creative department. It’s a bit of a legacy thing, but I like to say it’s diplomatic. We’re Switzerland, in the middle and honestly it’s the right place for PMM to sit. We’re not chasing sign-ups and we’re not owning the product roadmap, so we can hold the line on the customer story across both. With that, we have a lot of creative designers clustered around the product departments, so every PMM team works with a visual designer, a 3D designer - motion where possible. We do the strategy up front, then very quickly get into what this actually looks like for customers. Most of us spend a lot of time in Figma. Brand identity sits within creative too, while the growth side of brand strategy and above-the-line execution sits in the growth department. We’ve gone from an agency model, with everyone requesting things and no PMM filter, to PMM owning the strategy before anything hits a designer’s desk. What do you think lets Revolut ship at the pace it does? It really comes back to the cultural values. Revolut is very clear about who it is and who it isn’t. Everyone is incredibly high agency, with a strong get-it-done mentality. Even though we’re big now, with a lot of process and compliance as a bank, people bring a startup mentality: all hands on deck, small lean teams, a flat hierarchy. There’s a genuinely entrepreneurial streak to it. A flat hierarchy means nobody’s waiting for permission, so people treat their product like a business they own rather than a brief they’ve been handed. Nobody says “that’s not my job, I just do the product marketing bit.” The way we work is that the KPI will be around product usage, and then we leave it to the individual PMM to decide how they want to go and drive that. You get a heck of a lot of autonomy. For the right people that’s exciting. For the wrong people it’s daunting. You’re not just shipping the product, you’re constantly looking at it through a business lens. So there’s less soul-searching about what PMM should be measured on? We’ve tried every possible combination of KPIs during my time here, and we always land in the same place: what is the purpose of PMM at Revolut? It’s two things. Are people using the product, and is the GTM excellent? So we’ve built the KPIs around that: new users to a product, driven by marketing, assessed against holdout groups. Then recurring users, because - for example - we don’t just want you to open a savings account, we want you to put money into it. And we look at the GPPU ( Gross Profit Per User) uplift alongside that, the actual commercial impact. Attributing GPPU directly to PMM is something most teams in our discipline never crack, so building that with internal teams was a real unlock. GTM excellence used to be the subjective bit, but with our data and ops team we’ve built a “GTM Excellence” score: click-through rate, overall conversions, and a low-weighted element of stakeholder feedback - almost an exec-level NPS. A lot of that model exists to stop us celebrating a big launch spike and then never looking at the product again until the next GTM. You want it out in the world, taking care of itself while you monitor it, so you can move on and fix another part of the funnel. Does the rest of the business actually understand what product marketing is? Across the business, yes, and that surprised me when I joined. I thought I’d be living in dashboards and SQL. But everyone here is so brilliant technically that while the dashboards are key, where we add the most value is the creativity. Within fintech I very rarely see work and think “wow, that’s inspiring.” You usually have to look further afield and be good at connecting the dots, and that value on creativity comes right from the top. I’ve had the odd sceptical product person who hasn’t worked with PMM before. Generally you do one GTM with them and it’s fine. You just need that one, “let me prove it to you” moment. Now we’ve got so many examples, plus clear metrics, that I’ve never had to do much of the “what PMM is and isn’t” tour you have to do elsewhere. You’ve been talking about AI in product marketing. What’s actually working, and what isn’t? The honest summary is AI has raised the floor, not the ceiling. It takes the mechanical work off the team so we spend more time on the parts that actually differentiate us. We experiment a lot. The strongest, most established example is a targeting model, built closely with the tech team, that gets us the right product to the right customer at the right time. We used to do that very manually, a lot of Boolean logic and SQL. The more interesting shift is that the model has flipped how we work. It doesn’t just match existing value props to customers, it surfaces clusters of customers it’s trying to serve where we’ve got nothing to dispatch. It turns the value proposition library into something we engineer against real audience gaps. Day to day, there’s a lot of creative ideation and mocking things up in Figma Weave . And one of my favourites: value prop validation used to be slow and hard to do at scale, but with Maze and AI-moderated user testing, the kind where people actually speak back to you, I can validate globally within 24 hours. It’s far more valuable than surveys: you get the clips, hear the language people use, and might realise you’ve got a term slightly wrong. What AI can’t do is the last mile of craft. The gap between what I picture, what I can get to purely using AI tools, and what our designers actually produce, especially with motion, is still miles apart. AI can get you a fast, passable version of almost anything, which is exactly why the passable version is now worthless. When everyone can generate their own, the work that stands out is the work someone has actually sweated over. That bar has gone up, not down. Revolut scaled across so many markets so fast. What’s PMM’s role in that? PMMs are largely global, and at our scale you have to build with a global denominator, a wedge that’s fairly consistent everywhere. The part that gets localised should be the proof of the product, not the story. So it’s one story that’s true in all the different places, addressing a real friction in each market, rather than lots of stories stitched together. What’s newer is that we’ve hired our first country-specific PMMs. We’ve got one covering the whole of APAC, and we’re recruiting for the Americas . They look across those markets and close the feedback loop. Being global is all very well, but once you’re on the ground you get a different perspective. I want the local teams to tell me if the central thinking is wrong. That’s the whole point of the role. That’s the bit we’re working on now: not just product parity, but what actually matters to this audience, before any positioning or creative work is done. How systematic is all this? Do you believe in playbooks and templates? Pretty systematic, though I used to be more anti-process. The second I write something down here it goes out of date, because we move so quickly. But to keep up with the volume, you need it. We have a very well-modelled GTM process - about ten steps. It’s a bit of a GTM Bible that has evolved over years. Any time I have a new learning or spot a gap, it gets updated in there. Alongside it we have GTM tiering for channel decisions, plus value prop and GTM strategy templates that feed a proper value proposition library. Where we lean into playbooks most is repeatable, sequential launches. New partnerships on plans, for example, are playbooked so local teams and ops can pick them up, adjust, and get PMM review. I wouldn’t do that for the big things. Those are too important to copy-and-paste. The whole point is to free up effort for the new bets and the work built from scratch. Reflecting on your time running PMM at Revolut, what are you most pleased about, and what excites you next? The thing I didn’t expect is how much the calibre of the team compounds. When everyone around you is genuinely excellent, the bar for your own work quietly goes up, and that’s been the most rewarding part to protect as we’ve scaled - not letting that slip even as the headcount grows. Second, the measurability. Attributing GPPU directly from conversions to PMM is a big thing, and a big challenge for our discipline generally. Once we cracked financial attribution, the risk was over-indexing on it. Some of the most important PMM work will never show up in a GPPU number. The story, the craft and the willingness to try something that’s never been done before, none of that attributes cleanly, and we protect time for it deliberately. Third, the creativity - the never-settle instinct. Whether it’s a tiny GTM or something as simple as a product article, we’re all conscious of whether it’s the best it could be. What excites me next is cracking that local nuance at scale, keeping the global model working while getting genuinely sharp on individual markets. No small challenge, but it’s the one I’m most keen to solve. If this sounds like your ideal PMM set up, you’ll find a number of roles at Revolut live on PMMJobs.co right now.
